card:
$25 an hour = $52,000 a year.

Take-home: about $3,660/month

Rent: $1,650
Car + insurance: $725
Groceries: $420
Utilities + phone: $290
Gas: $165
Health insurance: $140
Student loan: $300

Total: $3,690

What's left?

-$30.

Before an oil change. Before a birthday gift. Before a single dollar saved.
caption:
$25 an hour sounds like a solid paycheck. Then the bills show up.

On paper, $52,000 a year is close to the middle of the road. After federal tax and FICA, it comes out to about $3,660 a month in a state with no income tax. Less if your state takes a cut.

Now line up the basics. Rent near the national average. A used car payment plus full coverage insurance. Groceries for one. Health insurance through work. A typical student loan payment.

The math lands $30 in the red. Every month.

What nobody tells you: this isn't a latte problem. Every line here is a normal, average cost.

A few moves that can actually help:

• Shop car insurance every renewal (rates vary by hundreds)
• Check if your student loan qualifies for a lower income-based payment
• Ask about the employer 401(k) match before skipping it, since it's free money
• Push for a raise with local pay data in hand
• Consider a roommate or a cheaper area at lease renewal

Which line in this budget hits the hardest where you live?

#JustMoney #CostOfLiving #Budgeting

card:
Grandpa buys a rental building for $120k. Today it's worth $4M.

Grandpa doesn't sell because selling triggers a huge tax bill.

Grandpa borrows against it instead. A loan isn't income. So no tax.

Grandpa lives off the loans for decades while the rent covers the interest.

Grandpa dies still owning the building. The kids inherit it at a $4M basis. They sell, pay off the loans & owe nothing on the gain.

The $3.88M gain? Never taxed.

This is how wealthy families avoid taxes & build generational wealth.
caption:
Wealthy families have a three-word strategy: buy, borrow, die.

It sounds like a loophole. It's actually just how the tax code works.

Here's the logic. Selling an asset that went up in value triggers capital gains tax. Borrowing against it doesn't, because a loan isn't income. And when the owner passes away, the heirs get a "step-up in basis," meaning the asset is treated as if they bought it at today's value.

So decades of growth can be passed down without anyone ever paying tax on the gain.

What nobody tells you: the same step-up rule applies to regular families too. A house, a brokerage account, or a small rental can all get it.

Ways to use the same rules on a normal budget:

• Hold appreciated investments long term instead of trading them
• Keep a will and up-to-date beneficiaries on every account
• Think twice before gifting appreciated assets while alive (gifts don't get the step-up)
• Talk to a tax pro before selling inherited property

Did anyone ever explain the step-up rule growing up?

#JustMoney #GenerationalWealth #Taxes

card:
The federal minimum wage has been $7.25 since July 2009.

17 years. Not one raise.

Just to keep up with inflation, it would need to be over $11 today.

Full time at $7.25 is $15,080 a year.

A typical one-bedroom costs about $18,000 a year.

Rent alone costs more than the whole paycheck.
caption:
The federal minimum wage hasn't moved since July 2009.

That's the longest stretch without an increase since the minimum wage was created in 1938.

Meanwhile, prices kept climbing. $7.25 in 2009 had about the same buying power as $11 and change today. So every year it stays frozen, it quietly turns into a pay cut.

Full time at $7.25 works out to $15,080 a year before taxes. The typical one-bedroom apartment runs around $1,500 a month. That's roughly $18,000 a year just for rent.

What nobody tells you: many states and cities have set their own higher minimums. Around 20 states still use the federal $7.25.

If you're early in your career:

• Look up your state and city minimum wage (it may be higher than your pay)
• Compare pay for the same job in nearby cities
• Ask about raises tied to certifications or skills
• Track every raise against inflation, not just against last year's number

What do you think the minimum wage should be today?

card:
Your 2027 retirement limits are out (IRS, Nov 12):

401(k): $25,500 (up $1,000)
Catch-up 50+: $8,500 (up $500)
Catch-up ages 60 to 63: $11,750
IRA: $7,500 (same)
IRA catch-up 50+: $1,100 (same)
Full Roth IRA if income is under $158,000 single or $250,000 married

To max a 401(k) in 2027: about $2,125 a month.
caption:
The IRS just raised how much you can save for retirement in 2027.

The 401(k) limit goes up $1,000 to $25,500. Workers 50 and older can add another $8,500 on top. Ages 60 to 63 get an even bigger catch-up of $11,750.

The IRA limit stays at $7,500, but the income limits for a full Roth IRA contribution went up. Singles can earn up to $158,000 and married couples up to $250,000 and still contribute the full amount.

What nobody tells you: you don't need to max anything to win. Even getting the full employer match puts you ahead of a lot of people.

Simple ways to use the new limits:

1. Bump your 401(k) by 1% on January 1
2. Make sure you're getting the full employer match
3. Set up an automatic monthly transfer into an IRA
4. Check if your income qualifies for a Roth IRA

These limits apply to 2027 contributions. Not tax advice, just the numbers.

What percent of your paycheck goes to retirement right now?

#JustMoney #401k #Retirement

card:
Renters get told they're "throwing money away."

Buy the median home ($416,700) with 20% down at 7.11%:

Interest: about $1,975/month
Property tax: about $350
Insurance: about $200
Maintenance: about $350

That's about $2,875 a month that builds ZERO equity.

The part that actually pays down the house? About $270.

Owners throw money away too. It just has a nicer name.
caption:
"Renting is throwing money away" might be the most repeated money advice out there.

But owning has its own money that disappears every month.

Take the median US home at $416,700. Put 20% down and lock in today's average rate of 7.11%. In the first month, about $1,975 of the payment goes to interest. Add property tax, homeowners insurance, and a basic maintenance budget, and close to $2,875 a month never turns into equity.

Only about $270 of that first payment actually pays down the loan.

What nobody tells you: the real comparison is unrecoverable costs vs unrecoverable costs. Rent vs interest, taxes, insurance, and upkeep.

Before deciding to rent or buy:

• Add up the true monthly cost of owning, not just the mortgage
• Plan to stay at least 5 years so closing costs pay off
• Keep an emergency fund for repairs
• Invest the difference if renting is cheaper

Buying can still be a great move. It just isn't automatically the smarter one.

Which would you choose at today's rates?

#JustMoney #RentVsBuy #RealEstate

card:
Got a 3% raise this year?

Prices are up 3.7% over the last year.

That's not a raise. That's a pay cut with a nicer email.

On $60,000, a 3% raise is $1,800.

Just to break even, it needed to be $2,220.
caption:
A raise that's smaller than inflation is a pay cut with a nicer email.

The latest annual inflation reading came in at 3.7%. So a 3% raise means the same paycheck buys a little less than it did a year ago.

On a $60,000 salary, 3% is $1,800. Just keeping pace with prices would have taken $2,220.

What nobody tells you: companies plan raise budgets months in advance. By the time the review happens, the number is usually set.

How to get ahead of it:

1. Track your wins all year, with numbers
2. Look up market pay for your role before review season
3. Bring the inflation rate into the conversation
4. Ask what it takes to reach the next pay band
5. If the answer stays no, quietly test the job market

A raise should be measured against prices, not against last year's paycheck.

Did your last raise beat inflation?

#JustMoney #Raises #Inflation

card:
Social Security gets taxed twice.

Every paycheck, 6.2% goes to Social Security. On money that ALREADY gets hit with income tax.

Then you retire, and up to 85% of the benefit can be taxed AGAIN.

The income limits that trigger it ($25,000 single, $32,000 married) were set in 1983 and have NEVER been adjusted for inflation.

Taxed on the way in. Taxed on the way out.
caption:
Social Security is taxed on the way in and can be taxed again on the way out.

Every paycheck, 6.2% goes to Social Security. That 6.2% comes out of pay that's also subject to income tax, so there's no deduction for it.

Then in retirement, up to 85% of benefits can be counted as taxable income once "combined income" passes $25,000 for singles or $32,000 for married couples.

What nobody tells you: those thresholds were set in 1983 and were never indexed to inflation. Back then they only hit higher earners. Today they catch a lot of middle-income retirees.

There is some relief. Retirees 65 and older get a new deduction of up to $6,000 through 2028.

Ways to plan for it:

• Build Roth savings, since qualified Roth withdrawals don't count toward combined income
• Map out which accounts to draw from first in retirement
• Check whether your state taxes Social Security (most don't)
• Run the numbers with a tax pro a few years before claiming

Should Social Security benefits be tax-free?

#JustMoney #SocialSecurity #Retirement
